extracted.intended_audience: social media influencers and endorsers who work with brands
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for when and how social media influencers must disclose material connections with brands so endorsements are not deceptive under U.S. law. Covers what counts as a connection, placement and wording of disclosures, platform-specific advice, and related truthfulness rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material connection / when to disclose
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have any financial, employment, personal, or family relationship with a brand, your endorsement message should make it obvious that you have a relationship (“material connection”) with the brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A “material connection” includes personal, family, or employment relationships or a financial relationship (such as being paid or getting free or discounted products or services). Don’t assume followers already know about your brand relationships. Make disclosures even if you think your evaluations are unbiased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial relationship includes anything of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial relationships aren’t limited to money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose the relationship if you got anything of value to mention a product. If a brand gives you free or discounted products or other perks and then you mention one of its products, make a disclosure even if you weren’t asked to mention that product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement: make disclosures hard to miss and with the endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure people will see and understand the disclosure. Place it so it’s hard to miss. The disclosure should be placed with the endorsement message itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures are likely to be missed if they appear only on an ABOUT ME or profile page, at the end of posts or videos, or anywhere that requires a person to click MORE. Don’t mix your disclosure into a group of hashtags or links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image/picture disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: If your endorsement is in a picture on a platform like Snapchat and Instagram Stories, superimpose the disclosure over the picture and make sure viewers have enough time to notice and read it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the disclosure is clearly visible on the image itself rather than only in metadata or captions that viewers may not see.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video disclosures (on-screen and audio)
rubrics_metrics.description: If making an endorsement in a video, the disclosure should be in the video and not just in the description uploaded with the video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viewers are more likely to notice disclosures made in both audio and video. Some viewers may watch without sound and others may not notice superimposed words, so include both spoken and visible disclosures when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live stream disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: If making an endorsement in a live stream, the disclosure should be repeated periodically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat disclosures so viewers who only see part of the stream will get the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple, clear language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple and clear language in disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple explanations like “Thanks to Acme brand for the free product” are often enough if placed in a way that is hard to miss. So are terms like “advertisement,” “ad,” and “sponsored.” It’s fine (but not necessary) to include a hashtag with the disclosure, such as #ad or #sponsored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space-limited platform phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: On a space-limited platform like Twitter, concise terms tied to the brand name are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like “AcmePartner” or “Acme Ambassador” (where Acme is the brand name) are also options on platforms with character limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague or confusing terms and abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t use vague or confusing terms like “sp”, “spon”, or “collab”, or stand-alone terms like “thanks” or “ambassador.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stay away from other abbreviations and shorthand when possible; ambiguous terms can cause disclosures to be missed or misunderstood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure language must match endorsement language
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure should be in the same language as the endorsement itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate or provide the disclosure in the language of the post so the intended audience can understand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform disclosure tools may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t assume that a platform’s disclosure tool is good enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using the platform tool in addition to your own clear disclosure placed with the endorsement message, rather than relying solely on a platform label or tag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-textual signals can be endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags, likes, pins, and similar ways of showing you like a brand or product can be endorsements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that actions which indicate support or preference for a brand may create a material connection that should be disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influencer responsibility to disclose and comply
rubrics_metrics.description: As an influencer, it’s your responsibility to make these disclosures, to be familiar with the Endorsement Guides, and to comply with laws against deceptive ads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t rely on others to do it for you. Review FTC Endorsement Guides and staff publications for more examples and details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and substantiation: no false or unproven claims
rubrics_metrics.description: You can’t talk about your experience with a product you haven’t tried, and you can’t make up claims about a product that would require proof the advertiser doesn’t have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you’re paid to talk about a product and thought it was terrible, you can’t say it’s terrific. Avoid making claims that would require scientific proof (e.g., medical or health claims) unless the advertiser can substantiate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: If posting from abroad, U.S. law applies if it’s reasonably foreseeable that the post will affect U.S. consumers; foreign laws might also apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both U.S. requirements and any applicable foreign legal obligations when posting internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-relationship disclosures not required
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have no brand relationship and are just telling people about a product you bought and happen to like, you don’t need to declare that you don’t have a brand relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement saying you do not have a relationship is unnecessary when none exists; focus on disclosing actual material connections.
